proposals.relationship: Bailyn identifies Pocock’s research among the resources used to reconstruct the British opposition traditions in revolutionary American thought.
proposals.evidence_note: The foreword reproduced in the 1992 enlarged edition, printed xii, explicitly places Pocock with other British political-thought researchers. Robbins, Gough, Laslett, Weston and other named scholars retain their distinct credit; no sole-source or general Cambridge-school lineage is asserted. The original 1967 copy and Pocock’s cited works were not collated or freshly read.
primary_locators: 1992 enlarged edition, foreword signed 1967, printed xii; PDF page 13, visually checked.

proposals.relationship: Wood recalls Bailyn’s seminar teaching him historical-mindedness as a way of understanding rather than accumulating facts.
proposals.evidence_note: Wood’s own 2021 interview answer describes his 1958 seminar experience and its intellectual effect. This supports a specific acknowledged teaching debt, without treating all students as a school or assigning Wood the separate recollections of Brown and Allison. No verbatim seminar record or complete later work was read.
primary_locators: Library of America 2021 interview, graduate-work question; Wood’s response, final two paragraphs on seminar questioning and historical-mindedness.

proposals.relationship: Bailyn praises Braudel’s descriptions but argues that separated temporal layers cannot by themselves explain historical interaction and change.
proposals.evidence_note: Own December 1981 address, published February 1982: the Braudel paragraphs and note 8 criticize the architecture of the Mediterranean study while valuing its evidence. This is Bailyn’s particular methodological judgment, not a rejection of every Annales historian. His earlier 1951 review and Braudel’s complete book were not freshly read.
primary_locators: AHA HTML, consecutive Braudel paragraphs before the discussion of cooperative research, and note 8.

proposals.relationship: Bailyn agrees with much of Stone’s narrative-revival account but argues for an explicitly evaluative synthesis that incorporates analytical history.
proposals.evidence_note: In note 10 of the 1981/1982 address, Bailyn distinguishes his aim from Stone’s account of changing fashion and qualifies any opposition between narrative and analysis. Agreement remains explicit. He states that he read Stone after drafting, so this passage is not made an influence claim. Existing collective route 672, from contextual history to Stone, remains unchanged.
primary_locators: AHA HTML, note 10, all three sentences/paragraphs of the qualification of The Revival of Narrative.

proposals.relationship: Colley values Bailyn’s Atlantic connections but challenges strong claims for their regional unity and the exclusion of early Asian connections.
proposals.evidence_note: Her 2006 review distinguishes praise for Atlantic inquiry from criticism of Bailyn’s stronger geographical model. The unity discussion at the end of section 1 and Asia discussion at the end of section 2 support this limited objection. Pestana’s book is separately reviewed; its claims are not silently assigned to Bailyn. No blanket rejection of Atlantic history or fresh reading of Bailyn’s whole 2005 book is asserted.
primary_locators: Publisher HTML, section 1 final paragraphs on discreteness/unity; section 2 final paragraphs beginning the discussion of Asia through the conclusion.

proposals.relationship: Bailyn credits Calloway’s account of Indigenous devastation but disputes its broad framing of the Revolution against earlier British imperial violence and Enlightenment aspirations.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1995 review: opening assessment, village-study qualifications and final contextual argument. Praise and disagreement coexist. Bailyn’s contextual defense and judgments about Britain, the Revolution and Enlightenment ideals remain his claims; they are not editorial findings that dispose of Calloway’s argument. Calloway’s whole book and any reply were not read.
primary_locators: Publisher HTML, opening four paragraphs; paragraph on nuances in the eight village studies; final paragraphs from the comparison of British violence through the closing tapestry argument.

proposals.relationship: As Rakove explains, Morgan’s account of the Stamp Act crisis supplied a basis that Bailyn extended through radical Whig ideology and changing colonial self-understanding.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Rakove’s 2020/2021 memorial discussion of Ideological Origins identifies the resource and two additions. The original Morgan studies remain unread here; this route claims neither sole authorship of the underlying research nor an exclusive source for Bailyn. It does not substitute Rakove’s absent individual endpoint or create a biography.
primary_locators: The Docket HTML, discussion of Ideological Origins beginning after the legal-history assessment, first three paragraphs.
